Remember this point: In spinning mills, these workers manage the machines that make yarn thinner from coarse stock and tighter from loose fibers through winding, twisting, and drawing.

It does not suit people who cannot stay active, dislike noise and dust, or hate shift work. Three-shift schedules are common, and a full day of standing and machine patrol leaves legs and feet sore. People seeking quiet office work will not stay long.

A common path is: textile factory apprentice or machine tender → start in winding, twisting, or another basic process → learn machine adjustment, yarn changes, and quality sampling → advance to equipment maintenance, repair, or team leadership, or transition to automated production-line operation.

This work suits quick-handed, attentive people who tolerate workshop conditions. If you can join broken ends rapidly, repeat motions all day without frustration, and work comfortably with machinery, you can succeed in this field.

Textile Winding, Twisting, And Drawing Out Machine Setters, Operators, And Tenders operate and monitor winding, twisting, doubling, and drawing machines. They complete yarn winding, twisting, and drawing processes and perform quality inspections and equipment maintenance.

entries: Textile winding and twisting machine operators operate and monitor winding, twisting, doubling, and drawing machines. They complete yarn winding, twisting, and drawing processes and perform quality inspections and equipment maintenance.
Set parameters for winding, twisting, drawing, and related equipment according to process requirements and start operations.
Patrol and tend machines, responding promptly to broken ends, wrapped yarn, clogged tubes, and other anomalies.
Change bobbins, join ends, apply wax, and clean machines to maintain smooth operation.
Sample yarn tension, twist, and winding quality and complete production records.
Assist maintenance workers with equipment repair and adjustment and report anomalies.
Follow workshop safety procedures and complete shift handoffs and production statistics.

paragraphs: After reviewing handoff notes, they patrol the machines, listening for abnormal sounds. They quickly join broken ends, doff full packages, change yarn, and periodically inspect and record yarn quality. Walking more than ten thousand steps in a day is easy, and peak seasons bring overtime to fulfill orders.

In one sentence: Tend winding, twisting, and drawing machines and keep yarn running smoothly. Tasks include setting parameters and starting machines, patrols, joining broken ends, changing yarn and doffing packages, quality sampling, recordkeeping, repair support, and shift handoffs.

AI will not replace textile operators all at once, but it will gradually take over monitoring and recordkeeping. Online inspection systems monitor yarn tension and quality in real time, while automatic winding machines join ends, doff packages, and change yarn. paragraphs: A score of 4/10 means automation is consuming repetitive actions, but skilled workers remain essential for exception handling, machine adjustment, and quality judgment. The score is not higher because production itself is shifting toward automated lines, making the next few years the operators' transition window.

Moderately high exposure does not mean no change. Intelligent winding and online inspection are already spreading. Operators who interpret MES data, adjust automatic winding machines, and understand basic maintenance are in greater demand and earn more at highly automated new plants.

Traditional machine tending is not a strong choice, but students can study textile engineering or mechatronics and pursue intelligent textile production. People with limited education should earn an automated-equipment operation credential and move toward newer factories.

Learn new equipment early, including automatic winding, online inspection, and MES operation. Transition toward equipment maintenance, repair, or production-team leadership rather than remaining comfortable with only joining yarn ends.

People without textile experience should prioritize newer, highly automated factories where learning is faster. Those with maintenance or electromechanical backgrounds have better prospects entering through equipment maintenance than machine tending.
When hiring for new lines, look beyond fast hands to people who read data, handle anomalies, and want to learn equipment. Retraining experienced staff costs less than continually hiring replacements.

The sense of security comes from simple, visible output. A package winds evenly and fully, machines run without alarms, and production records reconcile. For people who dislike complicated relationships and prefer dependable work, this certainty is rare.

This work suits people who prefer predictable machinery and limited interpersonal demands. Everyone tends assigned machines, keeps yarn feeding smoothly, joins broken ends, and completes quality sampling. At the end of the day, full yarn packages provide tangible satisfaction.
If you accept workshop noise and shifts and continue advancing with automation, this field will not offer high pay but can provide stable, dependable work.

Weaving machine operators manage looms and knitting machines that produce fabric. Winding and twisting operators manage winding, twisting, and drawing machines that produce yarn. One works at the yarn stage and the other at the fabric stage; the processes are adjacent but the equipment is entirely different.

AI will replace some purely repetitive machine-tending roles. Automatic winding and online inspection already handle end joining, doffing, and quality monitoring, shifting operators toward equipment management, data review, and exception handling. People who cannot use new equipment face the greatest risk.

On-site handling of broken ends and tangled yarn, machine-adjustment experience across yarn types, quality assessment by touch, multi-machine coordination, and immediate resolution of minor equipment faults.
This work suits quick-handed, attentive people who tolerate workshop noise and shifts and want to learn new equipment. People who cannot stay active, fear noise, or hate night shifts will not last.

Production workshops at cotton-spinning, chemical-fiber, knitting, and other textile companies, concentrated in textile clusters such as the Yangtze River Delta and Pearl River Delta and inland industrial parks receiving relocated capacity.

Pure machine-tending roles are not worthwhile, but they can serve as an entry point. During factory automation, learn equipment maintenance, repair, and operation and advance toward skilled roles and production-line management.
